title: Sit and Go Poker Strategy for Canadian Players
excerpt: Sit and go tournaments reward a different game from cash or MTTs. A strategy guide for Canadian players on stack sizes, the bubble and ICM pressure.
author: Jane Williams
bodyHtml:
Sit and go tournaments are the most underrated format in Canadian online poker. They start when the seats fill rather than at a scheduled time, they finish in twenty to sixty minutes, and the payout structure creates strategic problems that exist nowhere else in the game. For a player with an hour and no appetite for committing an entire evening to a large field, a single-table sit and go is close to the ideal format. It is also a format where a handful of specific adjustments separate winning players from breakeven ones, and most of those adjustments run against the instincts you develop playing cash games.

What makes a sit and go different

A standard single-table sit and go seats six or nine players, pays the top two or three, and raises blinds on a fixed schedule. Nothing about that sounds unusual until you consider what it does to the value of chips.

In a cash game, a chip is worth a dollar, always. In a sit and go, chips have no fixed cash value — they only determine your share of a fixed prize pool. Doubling your stack does not double your equity. It increases it by a smaller amount, because the prize pool is capped and the top prize is not proportional to chips held. This is the Independent Chip Model, or ICM, and it is the single most important concept in sit and go strategy.

The practical implication is that survival is worth more in a sit and go than accumulation is. A marginally profitable call in chip terms — one that wins chips slightly more often than it loses them — can be clearly unprofitable in prize-pool terms, particularly close to the money. Cash-game instincts push you to take those spots. Sit and go strategy says decline them.

Phase one: the early levels

Early blinds are tiny relative to stacks, meaning there is very little to win in an uncontested pot and a great deal to lose in a big one. The correct posture is patient and tight. Play strong hands, avoid marginal confrontations with deep stacks, and let the weaker players at the table eliminate each other — which, at low buy-ins, they reliably do.

The temptation to 'build a stack early' is the most common leak in the format. In a large multi-table tournament, accumulating chips early has real value because you need a large stack to survive to a final table hundreds of players away. In a nine-handed sit and go, you need to outlast six people. Those are entirely different objectives.

Phase two: the middle and the shrinking stack

As blinds climb, stacks compress quickly. Sit and go structures are designed to force action, and by the middle levels most players will be in the 10-to-25 big blind range where post-flop play becomes largely irrelevant and pre-flop decisions dominate.

This is where the format becomes essentially mathematical. With a short stack, your effective options are to move all in or fold, and the correct choice for any given hand depends on your stack size, position, the stacks behind you and how many players remain. The players who beat sit and gos consistently have internalised push-fold ranges and apply them without emotion.

  • Position dominates hand strength. Shoving from the button with two players behind is a wholly different proposition from shoving under the gun with six.
  • Stack sizes behind you matter more than your own cards. A big stack to your left will call wide; two short stacks to your left will fold almost everything to preserve their equity.
  • Blind pressure is the main source of profit. Uncontested blinds and antes at this stage represent a meaningful chunk of your stack and are won without showdown.
  • Do not wait for a premium hand. Blinding down from 12 big blinds to 5 while looking for aces is the classic way to convert a playable stack into a hopeless one.

Phase three: the bubble

The bubble — one elimination away from the money — is where sit and go strategy diverges most violently from every other format, and where most of the edge is won or lost.

When three players remain and two are paid, everyone's equity is acutely sensitive to elimination. That has two consequences. If you are the big stack, you can attack relentlessly, because the medium and short stacks lose enormous prize-pool equity by busting and will fold hands that are technically ahead of your range. If you are the short stack, you should be more willing to gamble than your opponents expect, since your fold equity evaporates as blinds rise.

The single most valuable bubble skill is the discipline to fold hands that feel strong. Facing an all-in from a comparable stack on the bubble with a middling pair, calling is often correct in raw chip terms and clearly wrong in ICM terms. Every player who has learned to make that fold has taken a step up in win rate.

Heads-up and the finish

If you reach heads-up, the ICM pressure largely dissolves — you are already guaranteed second and playing for the difference to first. Chip value becomes close to linear again, and the correct approach shifts sharply toward aggression: play a very wide range, attack the button, and stop worrying about survival. Many otherwise strong sit and go players are weak heads-up simply because they never practise it, and the gap between first and second is the largest prize increment in the structure.

Where Canadians can play sit and gos

Format availability depends on where you are. Ontario's regulated market hosts several licensed poker operators, and player pool size directly affects how quickly single-table games fill and which buy-in levels run consistently. Our guide to online poker in Canada covers the format landscape, and the 888poker Ontario review looks at one of the regulated options in detail, including tournament and sit and go traffic.

Bankroll requirements for sit and gos are gentler than for large-field tournaments, because variance is much lower when you cash in roughly a third of the games you enter rather than one in ten. A common guideline is 40 to 50 buy-ins for single-table games, against 100 or more for multi-table events. If you are building a game from scratch, our casino and poker game guides and the wider Canadian gambling news section cover the surrounding fundamentals.

The short version

Play tight early, apply push-fold ranges accurately once stacks compress, attack the bubble when you are big and fold more than feels right when you are not, then switch to genuine aggression heads-up. That sequence describes most of the edge available in the format. It is learnable in a way that few areas of poker are, because the decisions are few and repeat constantly — which is exactly why sit and gos remain the best training ground in online poker.

You must be 19+ (18+ in some provinces) to gamble in Canada. If gambling stops being fun, free confidential help is available in every province.
